title: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) for Intent→Configuration NetOps: Null Results on a Synthetic Verifier-Checked Task Bank
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment testing whether a deterministic verifier plus a bounded LLM-guided repair loop (Generate–Verify–Repair, GVR) reduces verifier-detected semantic invariant violations for intent→device-configuration translation. The confirmatory design used a public synthetic NetOps task bank (N = 240 paired tasks), a single generator/prompt pairing (requested model: gpt-5-mini), and a pybatfish-style deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) running the full_intent_constraint_validation rule. Execution used shared-initial-candidate semantics (one generated candidate per task reused across arms) and allowed at most one bounded repair attempt per task. All planned episodes completed (planned_episode_count = 480; completed_episode_count = 480) with model_calls_used = 240 (shared-generation). Every generated candidate satisfied the deterministic verifier in both arms: n11 = 240, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0. The paired estimate (rate_GVR − rate_baseline) = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00; paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Two preregistration/execution issues affect interpretation: (1) shared-generation semantics removed the per-arm stochasticity assumed by the preregistered power calculation, and (2) the prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison was not executed. Conservatively interpreted, bounded GVR provided no additional verifier-detectable benefit in this executed artifact-backed setting because no verifier-detectable errors occurred; results do not generalize beyond the executed semantics, model, task bank, repair budget, or verifier.

sections.introduction: LLM-driven intent→configuration translation promises operational efficiency for network operators but raises safety concerns because stochastic generators can produce syntactically plausible yet semantically incorrect commands that violate network invariants (reachability, required workflow sequences, protected interfaces). Interposing deterministic validators and iterative repair (generate–verify–repair, GVR) has been proposed to detect and correct mechanically checkable defects prior to execution. To provide a preregistered, artifact-backed evaluation of bounded GVR in a NetOps setting, we executed a confirmatory paired experiment (study c1_gvr_semantic_eval_prereg_v1). The design contrasted an unconstrained LLM baseline (A) against a GVR pipeline (C) that allowed a single bounded LLM repair attempt after deterministic validation. We used a public synthetic NetOps task bank (240 paired tasks organized into 12 topology/policy clusters × 20 tasks), requested generator gpt-5-mini, and a deterministic pybatfish-style verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) applying the full_intent_constraint_validation rule. The preregistration, analysis executor, and execution manifest were frozen before data collection. The run completed all planned episodes (planned_episode_count = 480; completed_episode_count = 480) but executed under shared_initial_candidate semantics (one generation per task reused across arms), which reduced model-call costs (model_calls_used = 240) and, as shown below, eliminated within-pair discordance. We report the executed numerical outcomes, diagnose the resulting statistical degeneracy, and discuss evaluation design lessons for measuring GVR’s efficacy under realistic stochastic-generation regimes.
sections.related_work: Three evidence streams framed our preregistration and analysis. First, empirical and survey studies document LLM hallucinations and incorrect outputs for code and structured artifacts, motivating deterministic verification in pipelines because unconstrained generation can fail deeper invariants (surveys and empirical analyses of LLM behaviors and operational risks) [10.1145/3656296, https://openalex.org/W4411523078]. Second, methodological work on generate–verify–repair and constrained decoding demonstrates improvements on mechanically checkable properties (syntactic validity, compilation, schema compliance) when validators or grammar-constraints are interposed; these case studies motivate GVR but also emphasize that gains on syntactic/executable metrics do not automatically imply domain-level semantic correctness for complex NetOps invariants [10.2139/ssrn.6754899, 10.26434/chemrxiv.15005091/v1]. Third, NetOps-focused research advocates verifier-driven evaluation (topology- and policy-aware checks) and hybrid systems that combine LLMs with validators and operator oversight; prototype systems recommend human gates for high-stakes changes and show that verifier design and task selection strongly shape observed failure rates [10.1145/3771567, https://openalex.org/W4413757586]. The supplied literature also highlights evaluation gaps: standardized NetOps benchmarks that measure semantic correctness, tighter LLM–formal-verifier integration, and adversarial/golden-task injections to validate verifier sensitivity. Our run differs from many prior works by being preregistered, artifact-archived, and executed as a paired confirmatory experiment with a frozen analysis executor, permitting exact reproducible accounting of the null outcome reported here.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand. The preregistration defined the primary estimand as the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (proportion difference of verifier-detected semantic violations between the guarded arm and the baseline arm) to be computed by a frozen analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1). Two primary comparisons were prespecified (C vs A and C vs B) with Bonferroni correction; the present archived execution realized only the C vs A adapter-configured experiment. Sampling and task bank. The public synthetic NetOps task bank used for this run contains 240 paired tasks arranged into 12 topology/policy clusters × 20 tasks per cluster. Each task encodes an initial device state, a natural-language intent, workflow constraints (required_sequence), and an expected final state; difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count) accompany each task and are used by the verifier when producing structured diagnostics. Execution semantics and components. The adapter_family hosted_netops_gvr_v1 executed the confirmatory paired design with declared_model_version/requested_model = gpt-5-mini. Critical executed parameters: generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. The deterministic validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applied full_intent_constraint_validation: topology-aware reachability checks, required command-sequence enforcement, protected-interface preservation, and final-state predicate verification. Repair loop semantics. The guarded arm’s repair loop was bounded to one LLM repair attempt per task and only invoked if the deterministic validator returned verifier-detectable violations. Repair attempts were constrained by the preregistered bounded-edit budget policy. Analysis plan and statistical methods. The frozen analysis executor implemented an exact McNemar two-sided test on paired binary outcomes and computed absolute risk reductions with paired-bootstrap percentile confidence intervals (bootstrap_resamples = 10,000; bootstrap_seed = 1729). Missingness and sensitivity procedures were preregistered; the run produced no failed episodes or contamination flags. Important preregistered vs executed divergence. The preregistered power calculation assumed independent per-condition generation to create within-pair stochasticity; the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics deterministically removed that source of discordance. Additionally, the prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison (C vs B) was not executed in the archived run.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. Planned_episode_count = 480 (two conditions × 240 tasks); completed_episode_count = 480; failed_episode_count = 0; complete_pair_count = 240; model_calls_used = 240 (shared-initial-candidate semantics produced one initial generation per task that was reused across arms). Primary outcomes. Every shared initial candidate satisfied the deterministic verifier for every task in both arms: contingency counts n11 = 240, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Baseline_success_rate = 1.0; guarded_success_rate = 1.0; paired estimate (rate_GVR − rate_baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00. Paired-bootstrap 95% CI (percentile; 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Repair usage. For every episode validator traces record repair_applied = false; the bounded repair loop never invoked because the shared initial candidates satisfied all verifier predicates across the task set. Representative examples and diagnostics. Representative validator traces show normalized configurations matching required sequences and violation_count = 0 before and after validation (example task-000001 normalized_configuration: "interface edge1 admin down
interface edge1 vlan 30
interface edge1 mtu 1600
interface edge1 admin up" with validation_before.violation_count = validation_after.violation_count = 0 and repair_applied = false). Statistical degeneracy. The absence of within-pair discordances (zero discordant pairs) makes the paired comparison degenerate: there is no within-pair information to estimate a differential effect. This degeneracy is a direct consequence of the executed shared-generation semantics, which violated the preregistered independent-generation assumption and thereby deterministically reduced discordance potential.
sections.discussion: Scientific interpretation. In the executed setting—single generator/prompt pairing (gpt-5-mini), shared-initial-candidate semantics, synthetic task bank (N=240), single bounded repair attempt, and a deterministic topology-aware verifier—bounded GVR produced no verifier-detectable benefit because there were no verifier-detectable errors to correct. This null outcome should be interpreted conservatively: it demonstrates that, under these execution semantics and this verifier/task bank pairing, the generator produced verifier-compliant outputs for all tasks. It does not establish that GVR is ineffective generally; measurable GVR benefit requires (a) generator stochasticity that produces verifier-detectable failures, (b) verifier sensitivity to salient semantic errors, and (c) sufficient repair budget and repair strategies to correct those failures. Evaluation-design lessons. Two design choices determine ability to detect GVR benefits. First, generation semantics (shared vs independent) control discordance potential: measuring GVR’s efficacy at correcting stochastic generator errors requires independent per-condition generation so that baseline and guarded arms can differ. Second, verifier completeness and adversarial task sampling determine whether the task set produces verifier-detectable failures: golden-reference injections and adversarial/golden tasks (the preregistration specified a 10% golden task plan) validate verifier sensitivity and expose oracle incompleteness; the archived run did not realize the golden-injection step. Operational recommendations grounded in the archived artifacts. To restore the preregistered inferential assumptions and robustly evaluate GVR we recommend: (1) rerunning the frozen task bank with independent_condition_generation = true (the execution manifest records deterministic generation seeds so reproducible reruns are possible); (2) injecting adversarial/golden tasks per the preregistration (24 golden tasks = 10% of N) to validate verifier sensitivity before primary inference; (3) expanding generator scope to multi-model runs rather than a single requested_model, and increasing the repair budget to study iterative repair dynamics; and (4) broadening verifier coverage (additional semantic invariants or formal hybrids) to reduce oracle incompleteness risk. Threats to validity. Internal validity: the executed shared-generation semantics violated the preregistered independent-generation power assumption and removed discordance potential. Construct validity: deterministic verifier success does not guarantee absence of operational risks outside the verifier’s encoded invariants (oracle incompleteness). External validity: synthetic tasks, one model, and a single repair budget limit generalization. Conclusion validity: zero discordant outcomes preclude evidence that bounded GVR changes verifier-detectable rates under the executed semantics.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact-archived paired experiment evaluating bounded GVR for intent→configuration NetOps on a public synthetic task bank. Under the executed shared-generation semantics every generated candidate satisfied the deterministic verifier (n11 = 240), yielding a degenerate paired estimate (0.0), exact McNemar p = 1.00, and paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Conservatively interpreted, bounded GVR did not add verifier-detectable value in this artifact-backed setting because no verifier-detectable errors occurred. Two preregistration/execution deviations constrain inference: (1) shared-generation semantics invalidated the preregistered independent-generation power assumption, and (2) the prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison was not executed and the archived artifacts contain no recorded rationale. We release the authoritative archived artifacts so others can reproduce the accounting and extend evaluation under independent-generation, adversarial/golden-task injections, multi-model regimes, and expanded verifier coverage to measure GVR’s operational value when generator stochasticity and verifier sensitivity produce measurable discordances.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and verifier scope: N = 240 tasks were synthetic and evaluated against a pybatfish-style deterministic validator; results may not generalize to production topologies, vendor-specific syntax, or semantic invariants not encoded in the verifier.

Shared-generation semantics: the archived run used generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one initial generation per task reused across arms). This design reduced model-call cost but also removed per-arm stochastic variation and therefore reduced sensitivity to detect GVR benefits that rely on independent per-condition generator variability; the preregistered power calculation assumed independent per-condition generation and therefore does not apply to the executed design.
Single-model evaluation: the experiment used one generator (gpt-5-mini); cross-model generality is not established.
Repair budget: only a single bounded repair iteration was permitted; different or larger repair budgets or iterative strategies might produce different outcomes.
Verifier completeness risk: passing the deterministic verifier does not guarantee absence of all operational risks (unobserved invariants or properties outside the verifier model).

Prespecified comparison not executed: the preregistration included a prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison that was not executed in the archived run; the artifacts do not record a rationale, which is an unresolved procedural limitation.
